# Rotation Matrices

## What Is an Orientation? {.smaller}

A **coordinate frame** $\{B\}$ attached to a rigid body is described by three orthonormal axes $\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \mathbf{b}_3$ expressed in a fixed world frame $\{W\}$.

. . .

The **rotation matrix** ${}^W R_B \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ stacks those axes as columns:

$${}^W R_B = \begin{bmatrix} | & | & | \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{b}_3 \\ | & | & | \end{bmatrix}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Each column is a unit vector of $\{B\}$ written in $\{W\}$ coordinates. Reading columns gives "where the body axes point."
:::

## The Special Orthogonal Group SO(3) {.smaller}

A rotation matrix satisfies two conditions:

1. **Orthonormality** — $R^T R = I_3$, equivalently $R^{-1} = R^T$
2. **Proper rotation** — $\det(R) = +1$

. . .

The set of all such matrices forms the **Lie group SO(3)**:

$$\mathrm{SO}(3) = \bigl\{R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} \mid R^T R = I,\ \det R = 1\bigr\}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
SO(3) is a group: closed under multiplication, has identity $I$, every element has an inverse $R^{-1} = R^T$, and multiplication is associative.
:::

## Basic Rotations {.smaller}

Rotation by angle $\theta$ about the **$x$-axis**:

$$R_x(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

. . .

About the **$y$-axis**:

$$R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$$

. . .

About the **$z$-axis**:

$$R_z(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

## Rotating Vectors {.smaller}

If $\mathbf{p}^B$ are the coordinates of a point in frame $\{B\}$, its coordinates in $\{W\}$ are:

$$\mathbf{p}^W = {}^W R_B\, \mathbf{p}^B$$

. . .

To go the other direction — from world to body — use $R^{-1} = R^T$:

$$\mathbf{p}^B = {}^W R_B^T\, \mathbf{p}^W$$

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Active vs. passive interpretation.** The same matrix $R$ can either rotate a vector (active) or change the frame in which it is expressed (passive). We use the passive interpretation: $R$ maps body coordinates to world coordinates.
:::

## Composing Rotations {.smaller}

Two sequential rotations compose by **matrix multiplication**:

$${}^W R_C = {}^W R_B \cdot {}^B R_C$$

. . .

Order matters — rotation is **not commutative**:

$$R_x(\alpha)\,R_z(\beta) \neq R_z(\beta)\,R_x(\alpha) \quad \text{in general}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Read the composition **right to left**: ${}^W R_C$ first applies ${}^B R_C$ (body → intermediate), then ${}^W R_B$ (intermediate → world).
:::

## Properties Summary {.smaller}

| Property | Expression |
|---|---|
| Inverse = transpose | $R^{-1} = R^T$ |
| Determinant | $\det(R) = +1$ |
| Columns are orthonormal | $R^T R = I$ |
| Composition | $R_{AC} = R_{AB} R_{BC}$ |
| Identity | $R = I_3$ (no rotation) |
| 9 entries, 3 DOF | 6 orthonormality constraints |

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Rotation matrices have **9 numbers** but only **3 degrees of freedom**. The 6 orthonormality constraints reduce the effective dimension.
:::

# Euler Angles

## Euler's Theorem {.smaller}

> **Euler's Rotation Theorem:** Any orientation of a rigid body can be achieved by a single rotation about some axis through the origin.

. . .

A practical consequence: we can parameterize any $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ with just **three numbers**.

. . .

**Euler angles** do this by decomposing $R$ into three successive rotations about (body or world) axes:

$$R = R_{i}(\alpha)\, R_{j}(\beta)\, R_{k}(\gamma), \quad i,j,k \in \{x, y, z\},\ i \neq j \neq i$$

## ZYX Convention (Yaw–Pitch–Roll) {.smaller}

The most common convention in aerospace and robotics:

$$R = R_z(\psi)\, R_y(\theta)\, R_x(\phi)$$

| Angle | Symbol | Rotation Axis | Name |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | $\psi$ | $z$ | Yaw |
| 2nd | $\theta$ | $y$ | Pitch |
| 3rd | $\phi$ | $x$ | Roll |

. . .

Applied right to left: first roll about $x$, then pitch about (new) $y$, then yaw about (new) $z$.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
This is an **intrinsic** sequence — each rotation is about the **body's** current axis. Equivalently, the same result is obtained by **extrinsic** rotations in the reversed order: $R_x(\phi)$ then $R_y(\theta)$ then $R_z(\psi)$ about **fixed** world axes.
:::

## Expanded ZYX Matrix {.smaller}

Multiplying out $R_z(\psi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_x(\phi)$:

$$R = \begin{bmatrix}
c_\psi c_\theta & c_\psi s_\theta s_\phi - s_\psi c_\phi & c_\psi s_\theta c_\phi + s_\psi s_\phi \\
s_\psi c_\theta & s_\psi s_\theta s_\phi + c_\psi c_\phi & s_\psi s_\theta c_\phi - c_\psi s_\phi \\
-s_\theta        & c_\theta s_\phi                         & c_\theta c_\phi
\end{bmatrix}$$

where $c_\alpha \equiv \cos\alpha$, $s_\alpha \equiv \sin\alpha$.

. . .

**Extracting angles** from $R$ (when $\cos\theta \neq 0$):

$$\theta = \arcsin(-R_{31}), \quad \phi = \mathrm{atan2}(R_{32}, R_{33}), \quad \psi = \mathrm{atan2}(R_{21}, R_{11})$$

## Gimbal Lock {.smaller}

When $\theta = \pm 90°$ (pitch straight up or down), the matrix simplifies and **$\phi$ and $\psi$ become indistinguishable** — one degree of freedom is lost.

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Gimbal lock** is not a physical constraint — the body can still rotate freely. It is a **singularity of the parameterization**: infinitely many $(\phi, \psi)$ pairs map to the same $R$ when $\theta = \pm 90°$.
:::

. . .

Practical consequences:

- Numerical instability near $\theta = \pm 90°$
- Cannot smoothly interpolate through singularity
- Discontinuous angle extraction

## Euler Angle Pros and Cons {.smaller}

::: {layout="[50,50]"}
::: {}
**Advantages**

- Minimal — only 3 numbers
- Intuitive for human interpretation
- Easy to specify end-effector poses
- Singularity-free away from gimbal lock
:::

::: {}
**Disadvantages**

- Gimbal lock at certain configurations
- Many conventions (12+ in use)
- Not unique (multiple angle sets → same $R$)
- Poor for interpolation near singularity
- Velocity kinematics require a Jacobian
:::
:::

# Quaternions

## Motivation {.smaller}

Can we find a **compact, singularity-free** representation?

. . .

**Axis-angle** representation: any rotation is a rotation by angle $\theta$ about unit axis $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (u_x, u_y, u_z)^T$, giving the Rodrigues formula:

$$R = I + \sin\theta\, [\hat{\mathbf{u}}]_\times + (1-\cos\theta)\, [\hat{\mathbf{u}}]_\times^2$$

. . .

where $[\hat{\mathbf{u}}]_\times$ is the skew-symmetric cross-product matrix:

$$[\hat{\mathbf{u}}]_\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -u_z & u_y \\ u_z & 0 & -u_x \\ -u_y & u_x & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Axis-angle still has a singularity at $\theta = 0$ (axis is undefined). Quaternions resolve this by encoding both axis and angle algebraically.
:::

## Unit Quaternions {.smaller}

A **quaternion** is a 4-tuple:

$$\mathbf{q} = w + x\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j} + z\,\mathbf{k} = (w,\, \mathbf{v}), \quad \mathbf{v} = (x,y,z)^T$$

. . .

For rotations we use **unit quaternions** — those with $\|\mathbf{q}\| = 1$:

$$w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$$

. . .

**Encoding axis-angle** $(\hat{\mathbf{u}}, \theta)$ as a quaternion:

$$\mathbf{q} = \left(\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\; \hat{\mathbf{u}}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$$

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Double cover:** $\mathbf{q}$ and $-\mathbf{q}$ encode the **same rotation**. Unit quaternions live on $S^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$, and SO(3) is the quotient $S^3/\{\pm 1\}$.
:::

## Quaternion Algebra {.smaller}

The imaginary units satisfy $\mathbf{i}^2 = \mathbf{j}^2 = \mathbf{k}^2 = \mathbf{ijk} = -1$, giving:

$$\mathbf{i}\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k},\quad \mathbf{j}\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{i},\quad \mathbf{k}\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j}$$

. . .

**Quaternion product** $(w_1, \mathbf{v}_1) \otimes (w_2, \mathbf{v}_2)$:

$$\mathbf{q}_1 \otimes \mathbf{q}_2 = \bigl(w_1 w_2 - \mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2,\; w_1\mathbf{v}_2 + w_2\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2\bigr)$$

. . .

**Conjugate** and **inverse** (for unit quaternions):

$$\mathbf{q}^* = (w, -\mathbf{v}), \qquad \mathbf{q}^{-1} = \mathbf{q}^* \quad (\text{since } \|\mathbf{q}\|=1)$$

## Rotating a Vector {.smaller}

To rotate a 3-vector $\mathbf{p}$ by quaternion $\mathbf{q}$, embed $\mathbf{p}$ as a pure quaternion $\tilde{\mathbf{p}} = (0, \mathbf{p})$ and compute:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{p}}' = \mathbf{q} \otimes \tilde{\mathbf{p}} \otimes \mathbf{q}^*$$

. . .

The result $\tilde{\mathbf{p}}' = (0, \mathbf{p}')$ is again a pure quaternion, and $\mathbf{p}'$ is the rotated vector.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
This is equivalent to $\mathbf{p}' = R\,\mathbf{p}$ where $R$ is the rotation matrix corresponding to $\mathbf{q}$. The sandwich product $\mathbf{q}(\cdot)\mathbf{q}^*$ preserves vector length.
:::

## Quaternion to Rotation Matrix {.smaller}

Given $\mathbf{q} = (w, x, y, z)$, the equivalent rotation matrix is:

$$R(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{bmatrix}
1 - 2(y^2+z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \\
2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2+z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \\
2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2+y^2)
\end{bmatrix}$$

. . .

This follows directly from expanding $\mathbf{q} \otimes \tilde{\mathbf{p}} \otimes \mathbf{q}^*$ and collecting terms.

## Composing Rotations {.smaller}

Two sequential rotations compose by quaternion multiplication:

$$\mathbf{q}_{AC} = \mathbf{q}_{AB} \otimes \mathbf{q}_{BC}$$

. . .

This mirrors matrix composition — read right to left.

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**Numerical drift:** After many multiplications, $\|\mathbf{q}\|$ may drift from 1 due to floating-point errors. Re-normalize periodically:
$$\mathbf{q} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{q}}{\|\mathbf{q}\|}$$
:::

## Spherical Linear Interpolation (SLERP) {.smaller}

Quaternions enable smooth interpolation between two orientations $\mathbf{q}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}_1$:

$$\mathrm{slerp}(\mathbf{q}_0, \mathbf{q}_1, t) = \mathbf{q}_0 \left(\mathbf{q}_0^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{q}_1\right)^t, \quad t \in [0, 1]$$

. . .

Or equivalently, via the angle $\Omega = \arccos(\mathbf{q}_0 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1)$:

$$\mathrm{slerp}(\mathbf{q}_0, \mathbf{q}_1, t) = \frac{\sin((1-t)\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\,\mathbf{q}_0 + \frac{\sin(t\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\,\mathbf{q}_1$$

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
SLERP traces a **geodesic** on $S^3$ — the shortest path between two orientations. Simple linear interpolation of Euler angles does not give the shortest path and can produce unexpected trajectories.
:::

## SLERP: Numerical Example {.smaller}

**Setup:** interpolate from identity to 90° rotation about $\hat{z}$, evaluate at $t = 0.5$.

$$\mathbf{q}_0 = (1,\;0,\;0,\;0), \qquad \mathbf{q}_1 = \left(\cos 45°,\;0,\;0,\;\sin 45°\right) = \left(\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\;0,\;0,\;\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$$

. . .

**Step 1 — find $\Omega$:**

$$\cos\Omega = \mathbf{q}_0 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \Omega = 45°$$

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$\Omega = 45°$ is **half** the rotation angle (90°). This is a direct consequence of the half-angle encoding $w = \cos(\theta/2)$.
:::

. . .

**Step 2 — evaluate at $t = 0.5$:**

$$\mathrm{slerp} = \frac{\sin 22.5°}{\sin 45°}\,\mathbf{q}_0 + \frac{\sin 22.5°}{\sin 45°}\,\mathbf{q}_1 \approx 0.541\,(\mathbf{q}_0 + \mathbf{q}_1)$$

$$= 0.541\,(1.707,\;0,\;0,\;0.707) \approx (0.924,\;0,\;0,\;0.383)$$

## SLERP: Decoding the Result {.smaller}

$$\mathbf{q}_{0.5} \approx (\underbrace{0.924}_{w},\;0,\;0,\;\underbrace{0.383}_{v_z})$$

. . .

**Decode the rotation angle:**

$$w = \cos\!\tfrac{\theta}{2} = 0.924 = \cos 22.5° \;\Longrightarrow\; \theta = 45°$$

**Decode the rotation axis:**

$$\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} = \frac{(0,\;0,\;0.383)}{0.383} = \hat{z}$$

. . .

So $\mathbf{q}_{0.5}$ is a **45° rotation about $\hat{z}$** — exactly halfway between 0° and 90°, on the same axis. ✓

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
This holds generally: SLERP between two rotations **about the same axis** stays on that axis and scales the angle linearly. For rotations about different axes, the intermediate axis traces a curved path on $S^3$.
:::

## SLERP: Where Is the Axis Computed? {.smaller}

In the multiplicative form $\mathrm{slerp} = \mathbf{q}_0 \left(\mathbf{q}_0^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{q}_1\right)^t$, the axis is explicit:

$$\mathbf{q}_{rel} = \mathbf{q}_0^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{q}_1 \quad \leftarrow \text{relative rotation from } \mathbf{q}_0 \text{ to } \mathbf{q}_1$$

The **axis of $\mathbf{q}_{rel}$** (the normalized vector part) is the axis about which SLERP rotates. Raising to the power $t$ scales only the angle, leaving the axis unchanged:

$$\mathbf{q}_{rel}^t \;\text{ corresponds to angle } t\alpha \text{ about } \hat{\mathbf{u}} \quad (\mathbf{q}_{rel} \text{ encodes angle } \alpha \text{ about } \hat{\mathbf{u}})$$

. . .

**In our example** ($\mathbf{q}_0 =$ identity):

$$\mathbf{q}_{rel} = \mathbf{q}_0^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{q}_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 = \left(\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\;0,\;0,\;\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \;\Rightarrow\; \hat{\mathbf{u}} = \hat{z}$$

. . .

In the **dot-product formula**, the axis is not extracted explicitly — it is preserved implicitly because the weighted sum $\alpha_0\,\mathbf{q}_0 + \alpha_1\,\mathbf{q}_1$ stays on the great circle whose tangent direction encodes $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$.

# Comparison

## Side-by-Side Comparison {.smaller}

| | Rotation Matrix | Euler Angles | Quaternion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Parameters** | 9 (3 DOF) | 3 | 4 (3 DOF) |
| **Constraints** | $R^TR=I$, $\det=1$ | none | $\|\mathbf{q}\|=1$ |
| **Singularities** | none | gimbal lock | none |
| **Composition** | matrix multiply | convert → multiply → convert | $\otimes$ multiply |
| **Interpolation** | complex | problematic | SLERP |
| **Human intuition** | low | high | low |
| **Memory** | 9 floats | 3 floats | 4 floats |
| **Numerical stability** | drifts from SO(3) | - | normalize periodically |

## When to Use Which {.smaller}

::: {layout="[33,33,33]"}
::: {}
**Rotation Matrices**

Best for:

- Deriving equations (Jacobians, dynamics)
- Linear algebra manipulations
- Expressing velocity relations
- Composing many transforms analytically
:::

::: {}
**Euler Angles**

Best for:

- User interfaces / teleoperation
- Specifying initial conditions
- Small-angle approximations
- Aerospace attitude display
:::

::: {}
**Quaternions**

Best for:

- Real-time control / estimation
- Motion planning & interpolation
- Simulation & numerical integration
- State estimation (EKF, UKF)
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
In practice: **store** orientations as quaternions, **display** as Euler angles, **derive** equations with rotation matrices.
:::

## Key Relationships {.smaller}

$$\underbrace{(\phi, \theta, \psi)}_{\text{Euler ZYX}} \xrightarrow{\text{3 basic rotations}} \underbrace{R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)}_{\text{rotation matrix}} \xrightarrow{\text{Shepperd's method}} \underbrace{\mathbf{q} \in S^3}_{\text{unit quaternion}}$$

. . .

Going backwards:

$$\mathbf{q} \xrightarrow{R(\mathbf{q})} R \xrightarrow{\mathrm{atan2}} (\phi, \theta, \psi)$$

. . .

The **Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ (skew-symmetric matrices) relates to all three via the **exponential map**:

$$R = e^{[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times}, \qquad \mathbf{q} \approx \left(1,\, \tfrac{\boldsymbol{\omega}}{2}\right) \text{ for small } \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\|$$

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
The vector $\boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the **rotation vector** (axis times angle). It is the minimal, globally-defined representation — but it too has a singularity at $\|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| = 2\pi k$.
:::
